## Reading R Output {#sec-r-output}

```{r}
#| label: setup-3-3
#| include: false
source(if (file.exists("R/setup.R")) "R/setup.R" else "../R/setup.R")
riders <- read.csv(data_path("rider_earnings.csv"))
bills <- read.csv(data_path("electricity_bills.csv"))
earnings <- riders$earnings
bill <- bills$bill
```

### Learning Objectives

1. Read the output of `t.test()` in R: test statistic, df, p-value, CI and estimate.
2. Check that R output agrees with a calculation by hand.
3. Choose the R output whose alternative hypothesis matches the research question.

### Concept

In Section 3.2 we found p-values for $z$ tests from Table 4. For $t$, $\chi^2$
and $F$ the printed tables give only a few areas, so we cannot read an exact
p-value from them. Statistical software calculates the p-value for us. The
p-value means the same thing as before: an area beyond the test statistic, in
the direction of $H_1$, now under the $t$ curve.

```{r}
#| label: p-calc
r_t <- round(unname(t.test(earnings, mu = 600, alternative = "greater")$statistic), 3)
r_p1 <- round(pt(r_t, 24, lower.tail = FALSE), 4)
```

**Example.** In Example 2.2.2 (rider earnings, $H_1: \mu > 600$),
$t_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(r_t, 3)`$ with df = 24. The p-value is the area to the
**right** of `r fmt(r_t, 3)` under the $t$ curve, because $H_1$ points to the right.
It is about `r fmt(r_p1, 4)`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pval-areas
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-cap: "The p-value as an area under the t curve with df = 24"
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Right-sided H1: area to the right of t_cal"
#|   - "Two-sided H1: both tails, twice the one-tail area"
#| fig-height: 2.2
#| fig-width: 4.5
pval_plot(r_t, "right", df1 = 24)
pval_plot(r_t, "two", df1 = 24)
```

### Reading R Output

R is free statistical software. In this course you do not need to write R code,
but you must be able to **read** the command and its output. The function `t.test()` carries out
the $t$ test for one mean. For the riders in Example 2.2.2 we use
`t.test(earnings, mu = 600, alternative = "greater")`:

```{r}
#| label: r-data-riders
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr vec_code("earnings", riders$earnings)
```

```{r}
#| label: r-riders-greater
#| echo: !expr show_code
t.test(earnings, mu = 600, alternative = "greater")
```

```{r}
#| label: r-riders-vals
o <- t.test(earnings, mu = 600, alternative = "greater")
```

| Line in the output | Meaning | Hand calculation (2.2.2) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `t = ` | test statistic $t_{\text{cal}}$ | `r fmt(r_t, 3)` |
| `df = ` | degrees of freedom $n-1$ | 24 |
| `p-value = ` | p-value | (from the table: $t_{\text{cal}}$ in the critical region) |
| `alternative hypothesis:` | $H_1$ used by R | $H_1: \mu > 600$ |
| `mean of x` | $\bar{x}$ | 644.96 |

The numbers match the hand calculation. Now the decision can be written with the p-value:

> p-value = `r fmt(o$p.value, 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is,
> the mean daily earnings of riders in Chiang Mai are more than 600 baht at the
> 0.05 level of significance.

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## The confidence interval in one-sided output

With `alternative = "greater"` or `"less"`, R prints a **one-sided** interval
with `Inf` or `-Inf`. In this course we use the **two-sided** CI, which R
prints with the default two-sided test:
:::

```{r}
#| label: r-riders-two
#| echo: !expr show_code
t.test(earnings, mu = 600)
```

```{r}
#| label: r-riders-two-vals
o2 <- t.test(earnings, mu = 600)
```

The 95% CI (`r fmt(o2$conf.int[1], 2)`, `r fmt(o2$conf.int[2], 2)`) is the same
as in Example 2.2.2. The test statistic does not change, but the
two-sided p-value (`r fmt(o2$p.value, 4)`) is twice the one-sided p-value.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Reading numbers in R

- R may print `p-value = 2.1e-05`. This means $2.1 \times 10^{-5}$ = 0.000021.
- `p-value < 2.2e-16` means the p-value is smaller than any number R can print; report it as p-value < 0.0001.
- In this book we round the test statistic to 3 decimals and the p-value to 4 decimals.
:::

### The Five Steps with a p-value

With R output, every number in the five steps is read from the output:

1. **Hypotheses**
2. **Level of significance**
3. **Test statistic** (from the output, or calculated by hand)
4. **p-value** (from the output)
5. **Decision and interpretation**: p-value = ... [<, $\ge$] $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we [reject / accept] $H_0$. That is, ...

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-3
ob <- t.test(bill, mu = 1200)
```

### Example

**Example 3.3.1.** An energy agency records the monthly electricity bill
(baht) of `r length(bill)` randomly selected households. It
wants to know whether the mean bill is different from 1,200 baht. R gives:

```{r}
#| label: r-data-bills
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr vec_code("bill", bills$bill)
```

```{r}
#| label: r-bills
#| echo: !expr show_code
t.test(bill, mu = 1200)
```

Use the output to (a) write the 95% CI and (b) test the hypothesis at $\alpha$ = 0.05.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

**(a)** We are 95% confident that the mean monthly electricity bill is between
`r big(ob$conf.int[1])` and `r big(ob$conf.int[2])` baht.

**(b)**

**Step 1: Hypotheses.** $H_0: \mu = 1200$ $\quad H_1: \mu \ne 1200$

**Step 2: Level of significance.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3: Test statistic.** $t_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(ob$statistic, 3)`$, df = `r ob$parameter`

**Step 4: p-value.** p-value = `r fmt(ob$p.value, 4)`

**Step 5: Decision and interpretation.** p-value = `r fmt(ob$p.value, 4)`
$\ge$ $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we accept $H_0$. That is, the mean monthly electricity
bill is equal to 1,200 baht at the 0.05 level of significance.

The CI contains 1,200, which agrees with accepting $H_0$ in a two-sided test.
:::

```{r}
#| label: yt-3-3
oy <- t.test(earnings, mu = 620)
```

### Your Turn

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 3.3.1

For the rider earnings data, a labour researcher tests whether the mean daily
earnings are different from 620 baht. Use the output below to test the
hypothesis at $\alpha$ = 0.05 in five steps.
:::

```{r}
#| label: r-yt-3-3
#| echo: !expr show_code
t.test(earnings, mu = 620)
```

::: {.workspace steps="full" method="pvalue"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 3.3.1"}
**Step 1.** $H_0: \mu = 620 \quad H_1: \mu \ne 620$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $t_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(oy$statistic, 3)`$, df = `r oy$parameter`

**Step 4.** p-value = `r fmt(oy$p.value, 4)`

**Step 5.** p-value = `r fmt(oy$p.value, 4)` $\ge$ $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we accept $H_0$.
That is, the mean daily earnings of riders are equal to 620 baht at the 0.05
level of significance. (This agrees with Section 2.2: 620 is inside the 95% CI.)
:::

### Formula Summary

| | |
|:---|:---|
| Decision | reject $H_0$ if p-value $< \alpha$; accept $H_0$ if p-value $\ge \alpha$ |
| One mean in R | `t.test(x, mu = mu0, alternative = "two.sided" / "less" / "greater")` |
| CI in R | read from the two-sided output |

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-3-exercises
ex <- list(
  A = t.test(bill, mu = 1200),
  B = t.test(bill, mu = 1200, alternative = "greater"),
  C = t.test(bill, mu = 1200, alternative = "less"),
  D = t.test(bill, mu = 1250, alternative = "greater")
)
```

### Exercises

**3.3.1** The electricity agency in Example 3.3.1 now asks whether the
mean bill is **more than** 1,200 baht. Four outputs are shown below.

```{r}
#| label: r-ex-3-3-outputs
#| echo: !expr show_code
cat("Output A\n"); t.test(bill, mu = 1200)
cat("Output B\n"); t.test(bill, mu = 1200, alternative = "greater")
cat("Output C\n"); t.test(bill, mu = 1200, alternative = "less")
cat("Output D\n"); t.test(bill, mu = 1250, alternative = "greater")
```

(a) Which output matches the agency's question? Explain.
(b) Write the decision and interpretation at $\alpha$ = 0.05.
(c) Why is the test statistic the same in Outputs A, B and C, but not in D?

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.3.1"}
(a) Output B: $\mu_0$ = 1200 and the alternative hypothesis is "greater than 1200", which matches $H_1: \mu > 1200$.

(b) p-value = `r fmt(ex$B$p.value, 4)` $\ge$ $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we accept $H_0$.
That is, the mean monthly electricity bill is equal to 1,200 baht at the 0.05
level of significance.

(c) The test statistic depends on $\mu_0$ but not on $H_1$. A, B and C all use
$\mu_0$ = 1200; D uses $\mu_0$ = 1250. Only the p-value depends on $H_1$.
:::

::: {.solutions-here}
:::
